client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away a few weeks ago. I keep zoning out at work, like I'll be in the middle of something and then suddenly realize I've just been staring at my screen for twenty minutes. I'm not even sure therapy can really fix grief, to be honest — it just feels like something that has to run its course on its own.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're carrying right now is real and heavy, and the way you're speaking reflects just how much weight that is. You're right that grief isn't something that gets "fixed," and I want you to know that's not what we're here to do — therapy can't take the pain away, but it can help you move through it without feeling so alone or lost in it. The zoning out at work, that disconnection, is your mind's way of trying to cope with something overwhelming, and we can gently work on understanding what you need right now rather than pushing against what you're feeling.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not totally sure what "moving through it" even looks like for me right now. Like, some days I just feel completely numb, and other days it hits me out of nowhere and I can barely hold it together at my desk. I guess I'm just worried that talking about it is going to make it worse, not better.
therapist: The way you're describing this — the numbness, the sudden waves — that unpredictability is one of the hardest parts of grief, and I can hear in your voice that you're carrying something that feels fragile and tender right now. Your worry that talking will make it worse makes a lot of sense, but research and experience actually show the opposite tends to be true — avoiding the feelings often keeps us *stuck* in them, while gently naming them can slowly reduce their power over us. We don't have to dive into the deep end; we can move at whatever pace feels safe for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that talking will help... but I've tried opening up before and it just felt like I was ripping the wound open wider without anything actually healing. Like, I'd leave feeling worse than when I came in, and then I'd have to go back to my regular life and just... hold it together somehow. I guess I'm scared that if I start talking about losing my mom, I won't be able to stop, and I'll just fall apart completely.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with a kind of urgency — tells me this fear feels very alive and present for you, even as you're trying to hold it together on the surface. What you just shared is really important: you've been hurt by the process of opening up before, and that's not a small thing — it makes complete sense that you'd protect yourself from that experience happening again. But I want to gently offer this: the fear that you'll "fall apart completely" is actually a very common thought in grief, and what we can work on together is building enough safety and support *around* the opening up, so you don't have to white-knuckle your way back to regular life alone afterward.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but I guess I'm just not sure what "building safety around it" actually looks like in practice. Like, the last time I let myself really grieve, I cried for three days straight and missed work and my friends just kind of... disappeared because they didn't know how to handle it. So when you say we can work on that together, I appreciate it, but you're also not going to be there at 2am when I'm alone and it all comes crashing down.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but fast, like you're trying to hold something back even as it rushes forward — tells me this isn't just a theoretical fear, it's something you've already lived through, and that loneliness at 2am is very real. You're absolutely right that I won't be there in those moments, and I don't want to pretend otherwise — but part of what we can actually build together is a concrete plan for *exactly* those moments, so you're not just white-knuckling it alone in the dark without any tools or anchors. What happened before — the three days, your friends pulling away — that was you grieving without a net, and that's a very different thing from what we can try to create here.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate that you're not just brushing past the 2am thing, because a lot of people do. But when you say "a plan" and "anchors," I honestly don't know what that looks like in practice — like, what am I supposed to do, make a list and stare at it while I'm falling apart? I guess I'm just skeptical that anything on paper is going to feel real when I'm in that place.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair, and I hear it — your voice is soft but moving quickly, like part of you is both exhausted and still searching for something that might actually hold. You're right that a laminated list isn't going to reach into that 2am darkness and comfort you — what I mean by anchors is something much more embodied, like knowing one specific person you can text without explanation, or one physical thing that has helped your nervous system settle even slightly before. The goal isn't a plan that lives on paper, it's something that lives in your body and your habits, so it's already there before the wave hits.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and it actually does sound different when you put it that way. But the honest truth is, I'm not sure I have that one person I could text at 2am without feeling like a burden — that's kind of the whole problem, that loneliness piece. And I'm trying to think of a physical thing that's helped my nervous system settle, but in those moments everything I've ever tried just feels hollow and stupid.
therapist: The way you're speaking — that high, almost stretched quality in your voice — tells me this part, the loneliness piece, might be the most painful thing you've said so far, even though you're delivering it with a kind of quiet steadiness. What you just named — not having someone to text without feeling like a burden — that *is* the wound underneath the grief, and it's really important that we stay here with it rather than rushing past it to find solutions. That feeling of being a burden is a belief, not a fact, and it's one worth gently examining together — because it may be quietly shaping a lot of what's felt impossible about this.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, that it's a belief and not a fact, but honestly it doesn't feel that way when I'm living it. Like, I have actual evidence — people have pulled away, conversations have fizzled out, I can see when I'm too much for someone. It's not like I'm making this up out of nowhere.
therapist: The urgency and pain in your voice right now tells me this doesn't feel like a theory to you at all — it feels like something you've watched happen, repeatedly, and that's an important distinction to honor. You're right that those experiences are real — people did pull away, conversations did fizzle — but in CBT we'd gently ask whether those moments tell the *complete* story, or whether grief made you need something that most people simply don't know how to give, not because you were too much, but because they didn't have enough. The evidence you're carrying feels airtight right now, and I don't want to dismiss it — but I wonder if we could look at it together, because sometimes the story we build from pain leaves out pieces that matter.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that explanation — that they just didn't know how to show up, not that I drove them away. But it's hard to hold onto that when the pattern keeps repeating, you know? Like, if it were just one or two people, maybe, but it's been so many that it starts to feel like the only common thread is me.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, paired with something that sounds almost resigned, tells me this thought — that *you* are the common thread — has been sitting with you for a long time, quietly building its case. What you're describing is one of the most painful cognitive patterns grief can create, where loss after loss gets organized into a story about your own unworthiness rather than about the very human failure of others to meet hard moments. I want to gently ask: is it possible that the common thread isn't *you as a burden*, but rather that you've been in profound pain during each of these moments, reaching for people who simply weren't equipped — and that those are two very different things?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that framing... but it almost feels too easy, like a way of letting myself off the hook. Because if I'm not the problem, then I have to accept that all these people just chose not to show up for me, and honestly I'm not sure which version hurts more. At least if it's me, I have something I can theoretically fix.
therapist: What you just said is one of the most honest and insightful things I've heard in this work — your voice is soft and fast, like you're trying to get it out before you lose your nerve, and I think you've just touched something really core. You're right that both versions hurt, and the reason you've been holding onto "it's me" isn't weakness or distorted thinking — it's actually a way of keeping a sense of control in a situation that has felt completely out of your hands. But I want to sit with you in that painful truth for a moment: that the people who should have shown up, didn't — and that's a loss on top of a loss, and you deserve to grieve that too.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I didn't expect that to hit me so hard, what you just said. Like, I've been so focused on trying to figure out what I did wrong, or what I could have done differently, that I never really let myself just... feel sad that they weren't there. It feels strange to grieve something like that, almost like I'm not allowed to, because part of me still wants to defend them and say maybe they just didn't know how.
therapist: The way your voice is moving right now — high and quick, like something just cracked open that you've been carefully keeping closed — tells me this is a real moment, and I want you to stay with it rather than rushing past it. What you're feeling right now, that sadness that they weren't there, is completely legitimate grief, and you're allowed to hold both things at once — that they may not have known how, *and* that it still hurt, and that the hurt deserved more than you got. You don't have to defend them in order to be allowed to feel the loss.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
